Reactor typeface, FUSE poster

Tobias Frere-Jones’s distressed sans-serif for the experimental type magazine FUSE, shown on its FUSE poster as white capitals that break up line by line.

Source
Fonts In Use: FB Reactor
Creator
Tobias Frere-Jones
Made
1993 (Fonts In Use; poster credit line); released by Font Bureau in 1996
Style
Grunge typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Dirty, angsty, raw
Evidence
Inspected the FUSE poster for Reactor as reproduced in Typographica’s review of the FUSE 1–20 book (1647 × 2340), and the Fonts In Use type sample (856 × 194), in scratchpad copies. The FUSE issue number was not confirmed. Not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Fonts In Use says Frere-Jones designed Reactor in 1993 for Neville Brody and Jon Wozencroft’s FUSE; Font Bureau released it in 1996, and it is no longer sold. Fonts In Use.

Chris Hamamoto describes Reactor as “inspired by a burning building and its ruins”, with lowercase letters that contain copies of other characters extending into their neighbours, adding distress “the more type is set”. Typographica.

Wikipedia’s list of Frere-Jones typefaces calls Reactor (1993–96) “an example of the ‘grunge typography’ style of the 1990s”, citing Ellen Lupton. Wikipedia.

Observed

  • The poster is black with a grey, smeared photographic texture in the upper half and a dark photograph of machinery or wreckage at the foot.
  • Five lines of white capitals, cropped at both page edges, read like an incident report: “…WER LOSS IN ENGINE 3”, “…TIONAL DOWN 95 POI…”, “…ORE INTEGRITY SUSP…”, “…RNAL STRUCTURE DAM…”, “…LTIPLE SKULL FRACTU…”.
  • The first line is only lightly rough; each following line has more specks, torn edges, and stray fragments, until the letters in the last line are hard to separate.
  • A final line, “I CAN HEAR IT NOW”, is set in yellow in the same face with little damage.
  • The small credit line reads “F REACTOR ® 1993 FONTSHOP INTERNATIONAL © 1993 TOBIAS FRERE-JONES” in a plain monospaced face.
  • In the Fonts In Use sample, the capitals are a narrow humanist sans-serif with ragged, splintered edges and doubled strokes.

Why it belongs

Reactor makes distress a function of the text, not a filter: the more you type, the worse it gets. The poster shows the style’s link between damage and content.

Borrow

Increase distress down a stack of display lines, so the page seems to decay as it is read.

Crop display lines at both edges of the page, as if the text continues off-screen.
